text:
During the inflationary pressures of 2022, we created our "MORTGAS" consumer misery index that is simply a sum of the price of gas ($/gallon) and the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate.

Our MORTGAS index hit a record low in the early 2020s when mortgage rates got below 3% and prices at the pump briefly got below $2/gallon.  Those days are long gone.

Gas prices first spiked in early 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, then they trended lower for the next few years until they spiked again this year with the US invasion of Iran.

Mortgage rates went from 3% up to 7% during the Fed's massive tightening cycle to address runaway inflation in 2022.  They too had been trending lower over the past few years, but they've moved higher again this year since the Iran War began.

Combined, our MORTGAS index is actually at a new record high right now, eclipsing the peak seen back in October 2023.  Consumers are feeling the pain as we head into midterm elections less than a month away.

The Financial Times
October 9, 2026

Putting the band back together is surely a great feeling, but a dubious corporate strategy. Starbucks chief Brian Niccol has considered a merger with Chipotle, his $41bn rival — and former employer — the FT reported on Thursday. However neat the match might seem from Starbucks’ corner office, it makes little sense for shareholders.

Niccol knows Chipotle very well indeed. Over long periods of time, debts tend to rise faster than incomes, creating the long-term debt cycle.

Even as people become more indebted, lenders freely extend credit because during economic booms, incomes rise, asset values soar, and the stock market thrives. People borrow more to buy financial assets, pushing prices higher and creating a bubble.

So long as incomes keep rising, the debt burden stays manageable. But this cannot continue forever. Over decades, debt burdens slowly accumulate until debt repayments grow faster than incomes. This forces people to cut back on spending, causing incomes to fall and borrowing to dry up—eventually reversing the entire cycle.

When productivity cant fill the gap, the only lever left is more debt... and the only way to carry that much debt is to debase the currency. That is why everything feels more expensive every year and why your savings never seem to keep up. 

Except now, for the first time in history, we have a way out.

AI and robots change the equation itself. They add workers that dont age, dont retire, get cheaper every year, and add productivity on a scale we've never seen. 

The catch is that it's now moving faster than society, politics or economics can adapt. Coherence breaks down. That is The Economic Singularity.

This is what my book, The Everything Code, charts. It starts with the framework itself, how debt and demographics got us here, moves through The Exponential Age and ends at The Economic Singularity. text:
By my measurement, the efficiency of intelligence output is doubling roughly every five months. 

This isn't the models getting a bit better... this is the actual amount of intelligence you get out of each unit of energy, doubling, every five months... and the doubling time is shrinking.

Nothing in human history has compounded like this. Not electricity, not the internet. And there's no playbook for it, because every institution we have was built for a world where things changed over decades.

This is what I call The Economic Singularity. Somewhere around 2030 to 2032 the machine economy starts moving faster than the instruments we use to measure it... GDP, earnings, the wage were all built for a world of scarce human labour, all pointed at an economy that no longer runs on it. 

Which means the years between now and then are the window. The whole game is to be positioned on the scarce side of the ledger before the old numbers stop meaning anything, because once the machines are running the machine economy the easy part is over. 

We have maybe five years...
